This is not a new version or remaster of Dawn of War. This is just a repackaged version of the original game without you needing to buy each standalone expansion. 

There is some tweaking you will wanna do to get this working on modern hardware and high resolutions (UI will be a consistent issue)

Step 1: get a mod to increase the zoom for the camera 

Step 2: install a mod for the soulstorm expansion that ports the campaigns for the vanilla game and winter assault into the soulstorm client (this will allow you to use higher resolutions)

Step 3: the graphics and sound quality by default are set pretty low. you will want to change those, and in additon youll want to set up the launch parameter -forcehighpoly

Step 4: head into the Local.ini file and add fullres_teamcolour=1 to one of the lines. 


If you're willing to go through all that, Dawn of War 1 is one of the finest RTS experiences ever made, and the modding community is absolutely worth a look.

Dawn of War 1 and its expansions will be forever remembered as the Emperor's Finest.

Better than DOW 2 and 3 combined. Get all the games up to Soulstorm then get the Ultimate Apocalypse or Titanium Wars mods.

Played this game when I was a kid off steam for years, shown to me by my father. He was really into Warhammer Fantasy stuff more than 40K, but he enjoyed this game, and the two of us played it a lot (along with similar games). He also got me into Warhammer Fantasy tabletop around the same time.

Fast forward nearly 20 years, and this game still brings a smile to my face every time I boot it up - and yes, the game is fucking brilliant in every way, but there's a bigger reason.

The past better part of a decade my father has gone through serious ups and downs with his mental health (which in reality had been happening all along, he just managed to hide it), and he's been on a upward trend of recovery for the past 4-5 years - and it's only really been in the past couple years where I feel like I'm finally reconnecting to him in a meaningful way, and it's because of this money laund- I mean great franchise of Warhammer. Earlier this year I got really into 40K tabletop (love of the lore for years and many co-workers/friends played it) playing as the Imperial Guard, and a month or so ago my father picked up some Orks to play against me (after a bit of coaxing from me), and ever since seeing his face light up with delight (or anger from me blowing his shit up) from that first game last month, well.

I felt like I was back as a kid, playing pretend army on our kitchen table with my dad - and it feels good guys.

No he's not dead or anything and yes I'm crying at this point and no I did not plan to share so much, but it all kinda just came out. So I suppose if you are on the fence about buying this game, it gets a solid pass from me. Give it a go with some friends, and make some memories.

Love you dad.

[b]This is a long review, so if you just want a summary of why I recommend Dawn of War Gold Edition then skip to the [u]Results[/u] section and reading from there.[/b]

Relic Entertainment works with Games Workshop to produce an epic real time strategy game that pushed the boundaries of the genre. Dawn of War offers economics, base building, military tactics, and unit management. 

[b]Story:[/b]
Dawn of War, the first installment on an incredible Warhammer 40,000 saga. The game is based on the planet Tarturus where Ork forces are out of control ravaging the planet and destroying Imperial Guard moral; but, how are they winning so easily? Of course the forces of Chaos are behind the whole war. Dawn of War is the story of Gabrial Angelos and Isador Akios and how they work together to figure out the whole reason behind the presence of Chaos on the imperial garrison at Tarturus. 

[b]Campaign:[/b]
The campaign offers an epic tale into the 40k lore with amazing twists and turns around every mission. Coupled with the amazing combat system, base management, and resource management this game really packs a punch. The campaign is divided into eleven missions which put you to the test fighting against the Orc Horde and the Chaos Might. As you progress through the campaign you work with the Eldar to defeat a common foe, but as the game dictates the Enemy of your Enemy is not always your friend. The game pits teams together, but at the same time continually draws them apart. 

[b]Gameplay:[/b]
This game was one of the first to successfully introduce rapid base expansion by requiring players to capture strategic points, which give the player a trickle of endless resources over time. The fast paced gameplay coupled with the macro and micro unit management really made this game a force to be reckoned with. Although the unit population seems rather low (20 personal – 10 vehicle) because the units are based in squads the real unit count is much higher. The battles seem more like full scale wars with you gripping to manage all your units at once. The best feature of this game (and all the Dawn of War games) is that each team is completely different. They have different units, different buildings, upgrades, tactics, resource types, hero units, and strategies. For example the Orc play completely different from the Eldar while both the Eldar and Orcs play completely different from the Space Marines and Chaos Marines. The only two similar teams are the Space Marines and Chaos marines which offer a good learners curve to Dawn of War by giving providing a basic approach to strategy: build barracks, build turrets for defense, use main base to upgrade to new “age” to receive better buildings, build power plants to get power, and upgrade units within armory, etc. 

[b]Teams:[/b]
There are four teams: Space Marines, Eldar, Orcs, and Chaos Marines. Each team poses different tactics/strategic elements which make you play them differently. The Orcs are based more around unit massing and rapid base expansion. While the Eldar are more about unit specialization and micro base management. The Space Marines and Chaos Marines are essentially the same team set, and fit between tactics of the Orcs and Eldar. Each of the teams units have upgradeable attributes which customize them for specific purposes: weapons, additional squad members, and squad leader units. Each team has special commander units which can be used as heroes buffing the team and supporting military units.

[b]Results:[/b]
All and all Dawn of War is a must get game. If you can play older games without constantly yearning for the graphics of the modern day games then you’ll enjoy this game. The gameplay is not outdated, but rather refreshing. As it seems most strategy game developers have diverted from base building, resource management, and mass scale war to simple micromanagement tactic games. I loved this game and all the installments so much I repurchased them all on steam. Despite that I still have all the discs, in functional condition, right next to me. 

Pros:
+Economic, Base building, and macro unit management
+Fantastic story and campaign (which is very rare in a strategy game)
+Amazing teams which each play completely differently.
+Fast paced gameplay which requires expansion to acquire resource nodes (but those nodes do not run out like in most games)
+Unit customization allows you to create squads for specific tasks
+Fantastic computer AI that puts you to your wits

Cons:
-Cannot play this game while having another monitor running (if you have two monitors the game will launch but every time you move the mouse to the edge of the screen where your monitor extends the mouse exits the game as if you are playing in Windowed mode).
-Lots of unbalances (don’t worry they fix all of these in the later installments)

Dawn of War is one of the first "real" Warhammer 40k RTS games to ever hit PC´s.

You get to follow Gabriel Angelos as he uncovers a major plot in the Tartarus campaign, this is the first game in a long series of Warhammer 40k games that was created by Relic while they where still owned by THQ, also the very first game where we got to see the Blood Ravens as they where created purely as a "PC Game" chapter.

Story wise the game is as good as you can do with an RTS, you get a deep sense of where Gabriel Angelos comes from and what his goals are as you get deeper and deeper into the game the story changes and there are some major plot twists all the time. 

Graphic wise Dawn Of War is an old game and that is visible, however SEGA (now owners of Relic) keeps supporting the game and recently even released a patch to deal with some of the issues that had been around for awhile, this is despite the fact the game came out in 2004 which makes it over 10 years old now.

Gameplay wise DoW is very straightforward, you build bases and kill stuff as any other RTS, however the way that Relic gave us the Warhammer universe with the Dawn of War series is amazing, you get a deep feeling for your chapter and your enemies, you get some great story and a great experience as you go through the missions one by one. 

Even now the multiplayer is very much alive and working very well, you get to pick between Space Marines, Orks, Elder or Chaos Space Marines which gives you a great chance for some epic battles, Relic even included the option to paint your own army and use it online. 

All in all a great game for old RTS fans and even more so if you are into the Warhammer 40.000 Universe.

Dawn of War is a fantastic modern RTS that measures up very well against the greats in the genre like Starcraft and Age of Empires. It takes place in the Warhammer 40k universe but manages to appeal to players who aren't familiar with the tabletop or lore such as myself. 

Dawn of War unlike most "older" rts games isn't focused on building or resource gathering. You gain resources automatically through capturing "strategic points" around the map and stealing them from other players. This encourages exploring the map and assaulting other players very quickly early on. Building is also done very early on so the majority of what you spend your time on is creating units and attacking players.

Combat in Dawn of War is done very well. Because there's very little micromanagement with resources and buildings you spend most of the game creating squads, upgrading those squads with different weapons and assaulting the enemy. Each of the 4 races are familiar but different enough so that you'll quickly pick out a favorite among them. Dawn of War's greatest asset is speed, games go by very quickly and you are always getting rewarded for the smallest of accomplishments like capturing strategic points. Which stack up greatly as the game goes on. There are also a lot of little details to the game like how Space Marine buildings are generated by being dropped from orbit. 

The real unfortunate aspect about this release (The original Game of the Year edition) is it's arguably the one I'd recommend the least. It only contains four of the core races (Space Marines, Eldar, Chaos Space Marines and Orks) along with only a single Space Marines campaign. I still do recommend getting it since it does introduce you to the mechanics of the game very well, and those races do port over to the multiplayer of the subsequent expansions. But by itself the Game of the Year edition isn't as impressive as Winter Assault or Dark Crusade.

I'm a huge RTS fan, but for whatever reason, I never picked this up until recently. I was introduced to the Warhammer 40,000 universe by way of the Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine third person shooter, which I greatly enjoyed. This universe has intrigued me since then, and I have tried to catch up with the more long-term fans of the franchise by reading up on the lore and such online. It's quite different from most fantasy; where magic and medieval type weaponry is common in fantasy, Warhammer has a refreshing spin on things, relying more on machinery and gunplay while keeping the magic and awe the fantasy genre offers to players. It also falls in the area of dystopian, which is by far my favorite genre of any entertainment, and it is interesting to have a protagonist in this game whose ideals and beliefs could be viewed as fanatical by our standards, but would be understandable in such a future where he serves beneath a totalitarian empire.

Moving on from the universe to the gameplay, Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War is an RTS that is unique in its approach to a genre that is tried and true. Whereas many RTS games focus on base building and annihilation, this game simplifies the base building and relies more on strategical points that you must capture for resource generation throughout the map. Each campaign or skirmish mission "gets going", so-to-speak, much more quickly than other RTS games. You spend less time buiding and more time moving your armies along the map. For those that find some in the genre to be slow moving in the beginning, Dawn of War brings a welcome change. 

Something else that Dawn of War does well that not enough RTS games do (sometimes at all) is reinforcements and upgrades. Where some games have you upgrade units from their respective recruitment centers and it encompasses all units of the same type, Dawn of War gives you more choice in how you want them upgraded. You can build a group of Space Marines, add reinforcements (making an initial group of four into up to eight), add sergeants later on, commanders, etc. In addition, with upgrades you can have a few men within the group upgrade their weapons, and the selection of weapons is up to you. You can have four rocket launchers, two rocket launchers, one flamethrower, and a laser pistol, or any combination between. This gives the player an ability to build up a small army for one intention (rocket launchers are great at taking out vehicles and buildings, for example), while creating another for a different intention (sending a differently equipped army to fight infantry). Even within firefights, you can reinforce your army if you possess the resources, giving the player a second chance in battle when most RTS games give none.

Lastly, it should be noted that I am a single player only strategy player, so I buy games like this for the campaign and skirmishes. In saying that, this game's campaign is fantastic. While somewhat short (eleven missions and about 15 hours of gameplay; note that Steam did not track all of my game time), the story is quite good and involving, taking you across many different types of landscapes and introducing you to different races to fight against. The cutscenes are a bit stilted due to the game's age, and the voice acting (while over-dramatic at times) is fantastic. The missions are vast and varied, and the game never gets in the habit of annoying you with time limits (I hate timed missions in any game, personally). The missions were challenging without being impossible, and they were friendly to both players who like to rush and complete the missions, and players like me, who like to leisurely explore the whole map and take over all positions before deciding to fully vanquish my enemy. Skirmishes are available, offering a few dozen maps that you can choose to play on, giving you choices as to what colors your army wears to which races you fight against, along with a whole myriad of other choices to make to tweak your gameplay if you so choose. 

In summary, Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War is a fantastic RTS title that makes me very happy I purchased the Master Collection of games, because I am looking forward to experiencing more of this interesting universe. I would recommend it to any fans of RTS, as well as those looking to get into the genre, as this game is extraordinarily user friendly and has a fantastic tutorial. If you are unsure, I urge you to try the demo. I played the demo some time before buying the game and loved what it offered, so it is a fair representation of the game. I can see myself adding this to a list of games I come back to every now and then, because it offers a truly unique strategy experience that stands apart from others. I went into this game with no expectations other than what I'd read through some of the reviews, and after beating it, I consider myself a fan.

The early-mid 2000s were a time when there had been a real shift in online gaming, particular in the PC world. The RTS market had dominated since the late 90s with such timeless classics such as Star Craft, War Craft 2, Command and Conquer, and Age of Empires. However, with the rise of games like Ultima Online and Ever Quest, popularity for these games were rapidly increasing, even in their infancy. 

Dawn of War might have been late to the party, but it was still successful enough to bring Warhammer 40k to the video game medium, with future titles in this series as well as branching into other genre. Whats great about DoW is how refreshing it still feels in the twilight years of the RTS heyday, especially with the mechanics that it brought to the table.

Though not as refined as previously mentioned titles, it's still game play stands out on its own and apart. You aren't bogged down with needing to create a factory of unit producing buildings and spamming hotkeys. The squad based system makes the game feel intuitive and fast, and resource management also lightens the hotkey load since you aren't mass producing gathering drones and scattering them across a map. 

The campaign is the best part of the game, in my opinion. It captivates you by throwing you right into classic fantasy  territory of Humans vs Orks, and introduces more prominent characters and races along the way. It's relatively short with only 11 Space Marine missions, but they're varied in their objectives and strategy's which makes for a more fresh play through, and is much less daunting compared to games like Star Craft and Age of Empires. 

The other races are playable through the games Skirmish mode, and though there's 3 others, they all play pretty much the same. The paint mode is fun but limited as well, with only a few units to choose from. 

Overall, if you're a fan of 40k, or a fan of  RTS games in general, its absolutely worth picking up. It has aged well, which I find true for most RTS games. You might be better off investing in the sequels, as they also have expansions to add to the game, but for what this is and at the sub $15 price tag, I highly recommend.

I'm the type of player that enjoys the spectacle of RTS games a lot more than actually playing them. I've never been very good at micro, mostly because I have no idea what micro means. But Dawn of War has always been a favourite, even pre-Steam, for the steps it took towards making an RTS accessible to anyone.

In particular, my favourite part of the game hands down is the way units are organized by squads instead of single units. Suddenly I, the idiot who can't wrap my head around Starcraft, can actually make some headway into smart tactical choices. In skirmishes around the map, it is faaaar easier to deal with 8 squads of units instead of 80 single boys. It also opens the game up to light squad customization and very satisfying upgrades on a per squad basis. More choices into what specialized weapons to take in each group of marines makes it so investing in the tech tree makes a real difference, especially since upgrades tend to change up what units work as counters to infantry, vehicles and etc. It gives a nice little nod to the types of loadouts you choose between in tabletop 40k, while providing a bit more depth and strategy in the unit matchups.

I'm also not much for mindless skirmishes, so it's nice that the single player story is a lot of fun too. Sure, it's SPACE MARINES only, but the mission design is cool and interesting, there's a nice slow intro to your advanced units, and you get a lot of variety in goals and enemies. The actual plot itself is typical 40k fluff, but the over the top voice acting is silly and fun.

The only real downside is that pathfinding is not very good, like most RTS games of the era. You can live with it, but there's plenty of maps where it just isn't feasible to send 70 orks into narrow valleys, since they'll just get caught on each other. It can be frustrating to fight with, but it's not an exclusive DoW problem so I can let it slide. The AI also cheats like crazy, but again, that's a common problem from the era.

It should be noted as well that there's a bit of fussing to do with mods to display in widescreen or higher resolutions, and there's weird artefacts and stretching if you choose to go that route. I recommend it anyway, check the guides/discussions for help with that.

In short, Dawn of War is a good RTS, but it's particularly great for people like me who want a chill way to watch marine boys smashing into ork boys and not get bogged down in specifics while doing so. For anyone who likes single player RTS campaigns, it's a great choice to pick up.

Never played this back in the day - apparently I've missed a lot, great strategy game! Can't play in widescreen, but 1280x1024 on a 1920x1080 monitor with integer scaling and forced anti-aliasing in drivers looks pretty great.

This game might be more than 10 years old, but it's still great. Afterall, some of the best RTS's came out back in the day.

A big emphasis is placed on being able to reinforce the frontlines quickly using forward bases placed on captured strategic points, and on using choke points in order to defend against pushes from armies that can sometimes be significantly larger and more powerful than your own.

As far as I remember, this game pioneered the cover and strategic point mechanics that were later on expanded in other relic games such as Company of Heroes. This is also one of the earlier RTS games to introduce squad mechanics, rather than training single infantry units at a time, and also one of the first to use realsitic scaling of units compared to buildings and vehicles.

Unit voiceover is great and really fits well within the WH40K universe. In fact, as far as I can tell (I'm not very knowledgeable in the lore), the game is quite true to the lore. If you crank up the scar decal and corpse settings in the graphical menu, dead units, blood, and craters accumulate on screen in a way few, if any, other games have achieved, giving you a real sense that a bloody battle is underway. And you really should be able to run this game fine even on max settings. It's one of the few games that didn't cause my low end laptop to struggle with everything cranked up.

Unfortunately, there are a few annoying bugs to deal with. First of all, the game doesn't support widescreen. Understandable considering the age. Apparently, with a bit of DIY tweaking its possible to get the game to run in widescreen, but from what I read this results in the image being stretched and distorted. In either case, I couldn't be bothered and didn't mind playing the game with the standard aspect ratio, although reading some of the text was straining on the eyes. What is less understandable, and much more annoying, is that loading a save that was done mid battle causes the background sound effects and music to cease playing, meaning that if you want to enjoy these sounds, you need to play each individual mission from start to finish in one go.

The camera controls are also quite dated and clunky. Combined with the fact that you can't scroll out very far, and that your armies can outgrow the screen space, it is often difficult to manage large groups of units, especially in the middle of a battle. This is further aggravated by the blocky map geometry, and poor unit pathfinding, causing units to get stuck on map features and on each other, even though it looks like there should be enough space for them to fit through.

Despite these drawbacks, I still highly recommend this game.

If you're a fan of real-time strategy games or the Warhammer 40,000 universe, I highly recommend giving Dawn of War a try. With its engaging gameplay, immersive world, and unique faction options, this game is sure to provide hours of entertainment. The use of cover mechanics and hero units add an extra layer of depth and strategy to battles, keeping things fresh and exciting.

While the game was released in 2004, it still holds up well today thanks to its strong art style and sound design. The game's expansions and sequels also offer plenty of content to explore once you've completed the main campaign.

Overall, if you're looking for a challenging and rewarding real-time strategy experience set in the rich world of Warhammer 40,000, you can't go wrong with Dawn of War.

Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War is a true standout in the realm of real-time strategy games, offering a rich and immersive experience that continues to captivate both Warhammer fans and strategy enthusiasts alike. Set in the grim, dark future of the 41st millennium, this game masterfully brings the brutal and epic battles of the Warhammer 40k universe to life, making it one of the best strategic games ever crafted.

What makes Dawn of War truly special is its innovative approach to gameplay. Unlike many other RTS games, which focus heavily on resource gathering and base building, Dawn of War emphasizes tactical combat and strategic positioning. This shift in focus allows players to fully engage with the dynamic battles and intricate strategies that the Warhammer universe is known for. The combat system is both intuitive and deep, requiring players to think critically about unit placement, cover, and the strengths and weaknesses of their forces.

One of the game’s most exciting features is the variety of factions available, each with its own unique playstyle, units, and lore. Whether you prefer the disciplined might of the Space Marines, the savage brutality of the Orks, the mystical power of the Eldar, or the relentless swarm of the Tyranids, there’s a faction to suit every strategic preference. This diversity not only keeps the gameplay fresh but also allows for endless replayability as you explore the strengths and nuances of each army.

Additionally, Dawn of War offers a unique level of customization that adds a personal touch to the game. Players can change the colors of their troops and vehicles, creating custom armies that feel distinctly their own. This feature, while simple, adds a layer of immersion that many strategy games lack, allowing you to take even greater pride in your victories on the battlefield.

The game’s visuals and sound design are also top-notch, especially considering its age. The detailed unit models, atmospheric environments, and booming sound effects all contribute to a truly epic and immersive experience. Every battle feels like a grand spectacle, with the chaos of war unfolding in stunning detail.

Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War is not just a great game; it’s a unique gem in the world of strategy games. Its innovative combat system, diverse factions, and customization options make it a must-play for any fan of the genre. Whether you’re a veteran of the Warhammer 40k universe or a newcomer looking for a deep and engaging RTS experience, Dawn of War delivers in every way. It remains a shining example of how to bring a beloved tabletop universe to life in the digital realm, offering endless hours of strategic fun and epic battles.

Dawn of War is the first RTS game I’ve ever played and finished, and it is perfect for that. This game served as an introduction to RTS and Warhammer for me and after playing it, I have an interest in both now.

	The story is incredible, because it’s a Warhammer game.  From the first glance at the Steam page of Dawn of War, it looks like a “cartoon game where you fight goblins” which is proven wrong immediately while starting it. Dawn of War is incredible with how it turns every race, even the orks into a gruesome and interesting side to play against (and as in skirmish!) The pacing is great, when you start getting tired of fighting the same faction, a new one will get introduced. [spoiler]The mission A New Lead has great pacing and sets good suspense before the Eldar get introduced. [/spoiler] The characters are great, especially the Force Commander and the orks. The twist is fine and not too big, but it makes sense. 

	The game has fun RTS gameplay, it’s not too complex but still at a pleasant depth. The cover system is useful for putting defending units at a higher elevation in combat. It’s fun to create several squads of Space Marines and then attack a base from several sides. Leveling up your base and researching new gear for your army is fun and rewarding too. This is strategy, and how you supply your squads is a major part. Besides that, Dawn of War is just basic RTS, which is fun!

	The music is incredible, it adds onto the might of each race, it adds onto tense combat situations and it adds onto when the enemies are starting an attack. You could be losing your base and then you hear the Imperium theme, and you push back on the enemy until the tide has been turned. Or you could be discovering the map without seeing any enemies, and then hearing a jolt in the atmospheric music, to see your base being taken over by an Unknown Force. 

	The locations throughout the game are fun, and the amount of similar locations don’t overstay their welcome like in other games. There’s a few city maps/areas, a few jungle maps and a few chaos maps. 

	The game’s difficulty is balanced, some levels are harder than others, but each are very enjoyable.

	I didn’t encounter any bugs throughout this game.

	Overall I found the experience great as the first RTS and Warhammer game I played through. Because of this game, I bought the expansions for this game, Dawn of War 2 and its expansions. I found myself somewhat enjoying the expansions for Dawn of War (I haven’t played the Soulstorm campaign yet, only skirmish.) If you’re anything like me (and not going to dirty this game) then you should play it as the first RTS and Warhammer experience.
